title: Do more people watch sport or play it?
description: A colony survey gives the numbers of people who watch and who take part in five sports, and the numbers are large. A scale is chosen from the largest value, the bar heights are worked out for a double-bar graph, and the pairs of bars are compared.
teaching_notes: One idea: the largest value decides how many people one unit stands for. Watch for children who choose a scale of one unit for one person, which makes the bars far too long.

video_script.why: The child can draw a double-bar graph and now picks a scale for large values.
video_script.substitution: The largest value decides how much one unit must stand for.
video_script.anchor: A survey of a colony. Watching: cricket 1240, basketball 470, swimming 510, hockey 430, athletics 250. Taking part: cricket 620, basketball 320, swimming 320, hockey 250, athletics 105.
video_script.payoff_line: In every sport, more people watch than take part.

final_answer.value: Scale 1 unit = 200 people; watchers outnumber players in every sport; cricket leads both, with players half of watchers
final_answer.spoken: in every sport more people watch than take part

maths_rules: largest value 1240, so 1 unit = 200 people fits on a line up to 1400 (7 units)
a watching bar and a taking part bar for each sport, with a key
in every sport more watch than take part: 1240 > 620, 470 > 320, 510 > 320, 430 > 250, 250 > 105
video_script.design: One pair of lists and one empty graph. The line is marked in units of two hundred, then the ten bars grow in pairs.

beats.on_screen: small title card From your book; two lists of numbers of people for five sports, one list for watching and one for taking part

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>This is a question from your book.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>A survey in a colony asked people about their favourite sports.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Some people like to watch a sport, and some like to take part in it.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>How can one graph show both numbers for each sport?

beats.on_screen: the lists and the empty graph stay on the board

marks.m1: Keeko sits at the corner of the board as the child

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: a vertical line with equal units; one unit stands for some number of people, labelled scale; two bars side by side with a key

marks.m1: a vertical line with equal units appears
marks.m2: one unit is labelled with a number of people and called scale
marks.m3: two bars of different colours stand side by side with a key
marks.m4: the hint line the same way as the book's example glows

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>A bar graph stands on a line marked in equal units.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>The number of people that one unit stands for is called the scale.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>A double-bar graph has two bars for each sport, with a key.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>We solve it the same way as the example in your book.

beats.on_screen: Given: watching: cricket 1240, basketball 470, swimming 510, hockey 430, athletics 250; taking part: cricket 620, basketball 320, swimming 320, hockey 250, athletics 105

marks.m2: the cricket and basketball numbers glow
marks.m3: the swimming, hockey and athletics numbers glow
marks.m4: the taking part list is written
marks.m5: the cricket and basketball numbers glow
marks.m6: the swimming, hockey and athletics numbers glow

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Given, the survey has two lists of people.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Watching, cricket has one thousand two hundred and forty. Basketball has four hundred and seventy.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Swimming has five hundred and ten. Hockey has four hundred and thirty. Athletics has two hundred and fifty.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>Taking part is the second list.
<bookmark mark='m5'/>Cricket has six hundred and twenty. Basketball has three hundred and twenty.
<bookmark mark='m6'/>Swimming has three hundred and twenty. Hockey has two hundred and fifty. Athletics has one hundred and five.

beats.on_screen: To find: a scale; a double-bar graph; observations

marks.m1: the three tasks are written one under the other

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>We have to choose a scale, draw the double-bar graph, and write what we see.

beats.on_screen: largest value = 1240; 1 unit = 200 people; the line runs to 1400 (7 units)

marks.m3: the line is marked to 1400, seven units

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step one, choose the scale from the largest value, one thousand two hundred and forty.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Let one unit stand for two hundred people.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Seven units reach one thousand four hundred, so the line is long enough.

marks.m4: the other eight heights are written

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step two, find each bar's height by dividing the people by two hundred.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>For cricket watching, divide one thousand two hundred and forty by two hundred. The bar is six point two units tall.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>For athletics taking part, divide one hundred and five by two hundred. The bar is zero point five two five units tall.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>The other eight bars are found the same way.

beats.on_screen: the double-bar graph: two bars for each sport, with a key

marks.m2: the taking part bars grow beside them

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three, draw a bar for watching in each sport.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Draw a bar for taking part beside it.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Add a key to tell the two kinds of bar apart.

beats.on_screen: pairs: 1240 and 620; 470 and 320; 510 and 320; 430 and 250; 250 and 105; cricket has the tallest bars

marks.m1: each pair of bars is compared

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step four, compare each pair of bars and write what you see.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Cricket has the tallest bar of both kinds.
<bookmark mark='m1'/>Step five, check the bars. Multiply a height by two hundred to get the people back.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Six point two times two hundred is one thousand two hundred and forty. Zero point five two five times two hundred is one hundred and five.

beats.on_screen: Answer: scale 1 unit = 200 people; in every sport more people watch than take part; cricket leads both; 620 ÷ 1240 = 0.5
narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>In every sport, more people watch than take part.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Cricket leads in both kinds.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>For cricket, six hundred and twenty divided by one thousand two hundred and forty is a half. Only half as many take part as watch.
